# Details

In this exam, you will be asked to answer questions about pre-written code; to fill in small blanks in code; or to sketch the output of a process or analysis. Your fill-in-the-blank answers need to be conceptually correct, not perfect. For example, if you fill in a blank with `mutates` instead of `mutate`, you will still get full credit.

You may assume throughout the exam that there are no syntax errors in the code - for example, you will not be asked to spot a missing comma, an unclosed parentheses, or a typo in an object name. There are also no "trick" questions - the code you are shown can be expected to run without error, unless specifically stated in the question.

# Part A - Complex Data Pipelines Sample Question

Consider the following two datasets:

```{r}
#| include: false

pixar_films <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/pixar_films.csv') |>
  rename(title = "film")
public_response <- readr::read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/main/data/2025/2025-03-11/public_response.csv')
```

A list of all Pixar films, with some information about them:

```{r}
pixar_films |> head()
```

Ratings from various film rating sources for Pixar movies:

```{r}
public_response |> head()
```

## Question 1

First, we want to add the ratings data from the `imdb` dataset to the Pixar movie list.

Fill in the blank to make this work.

```{r}
#| flourish:
#| - target: 
#|     - 'join_by\\(title == film\\)'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"

pixar_new <- pixar_films |>
  left_join(public_response,
            by = join_by(title == film))
```

## Question 3

Fill in the blanks in the following pipeline, which computes the number of Pixar movies released each decade receiving particular cinema scores.

```{r}
#| flourish:
#| - target: 
#|     - 'release_date'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"
#| - target: 
#|     - 'glue::glue'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"
#| - target: 
#|     - 'count'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"
#| - target: 
#|     - 'pivot_wider'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"
#| - target: 
#|     - 'cinema_score'
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"
#| - target: 
#|     - 'n      '
#|     - mask: true
#|     - style: "text-decoration: underline;"

pixar_new |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(release_date),
    decade = floor(year/10),
    decade = glue::glue("{decade}0s")
  ) |>
  count(decade, cinema_score) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = cinema_score,
    values_from = n       
  )
  
```

# Part B - Webscraping Sample Question

Wikipedia sites tend to contain consistent information across similar articles, usually in a box on the right. Entries about people typically include a picture of the person and their date of birth at the top. For example, here is Hadley Wickham's Wikipedia page:

![](images/hadley_wiki.png){width="70%" border="1" fig-alt="A screenshot of the Wikipedia page for Hadley Wickham. On the right side of the page, there is a gray box with a photo of Hadley, followed by a list of information about Hadley (e.g., birthday, alma matter, what he is known for, what awards he has won)."}

Consider the following function, designed to scrape the birthdate of a Wikipedia entry:

```{r}
get_age <- function(url) {
  
  my_html <- read_html(url)
  
  my_html |>
    html_element("table") |>
    html_elements("span.noprint.ForceAgeToShow") |>
    html_text() |>
    parse_number()
  
}
```

```{r}
get_age("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hadley_Wickham")
```

## Question 4

You notice that Dr. Bodwin is not famous enough for a Wikipedia entry, so this code breaks:

```{r}
#| error: true
get_age("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelly_Bodwin")
```

You'll also notice that some famous people share a name, such as Robert Gentleman, one of the creators of R. This also breaks your function.

```{r}
#| error: true
get_age("https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gentleman")
```

What would you change in the function to deal with these types of issues?

## Question 5

How would you make use of this function to add a column named `age` to the following dataset, named `r_people`? Specifically, what functions would you use and how would you use them?

```{r}
#| echo: false
tibble(
  name = c("Robert Gentleman", "Ross Ihaka", "Hadley Wickham", "Jenny Bryan", "Allison Theobold", "Kelly Bodwin"),
  position = c("R Creator", "R Creator", "Posit Employee", "Posit Employee", "Cal Poly Prof", "Cal Poly Prof")
)
```

# Part C - More Advanced Visualizations Sample Question

The following outputs show a summary table or visualization from the dataset `pixar_new`. For each, provide:

(i) what (if any) data wrangling steps are needed to prepare the data for this visualization,

(ii) the aesthetic(s) of the visualization *or* the `gt` formatting used, and

(iii) one *major* improvement you would make to the analysis.

*Note that a **major** improvement is something that changes the structure of the output, not just a different color, label, or stylistic choice.* At least one of your (iii) answers must suggest a different *geometry* for the plot.

For these answers, you may respond in either words or code. For example, these two answers would both be acceptable:

- `mutate(z = x + y)`
- "Add a new column named `z` that is the sum of `x` and `y`."

```{r}
pixar_new |>
  filter(
    str_detect(title, "Toy Story")
```

## Question 7

```{r}
#| echo: false

repeats <- pixar_new |> 
  separate_wider_regex(
    title,
    patterns = c(name = ".*?", "\\s*", repeat_num = "\\d*$"),
    cols_remove = FALSE
  ) |> 
  count(name) |> 
  filter(n > 1) |> 
  pull(name)

pixar_new |> 
  separate_wider_regex(
    title,
    patterns = c(name = ".*?", "\\s*", repeat_num = "\\d*$"),
    cols_remove = FALSE
  ) |> 
  filter(name %in% repeats) |> 
  select(title, rotten_tomatoes, metacritic) |> 
  arrange(title) |> 
  rename(Movie = title, 
         `Rotten Tomatoes` = rotten_tomatoes, 
         Metacritic = metacritic) |> 
  gt() |> 
  tab_spanner(
    label = "Film Score",
    columns = c(`Rotten Tomatoes`, Metacritic)
  ) |> 
  tab_header(
    title = "Original Movies and Their Spinoffs",
    subtitle = "Are the spinoff ratings always worse?"
  ) 

```
